Excellencies, distinguished delegates, youth leaders, I call to order the 3rd meeting of the 2026 Youth Forum of the Economic and Social Council. This afternoon, we will hold plenary sessions on youth leadership a critical force in shaping a sustainable and inclusive future for all. This session examines youth leadership as a central driver of a sustainable and inclusive future, focusing on pathways for youth engagement in civic and political processes. It emphasizes the importance of accessible and accountable participation pathways and highlight the innovative and emerging opportunities for political participation, including digital technologies, while examining limitations and consequences of the continued exclusion of young people from formal decision-making spaces. We'll first hear from the Dr. Felipe Polia, Assistant Secretary-General for Youth Affairs, who will deliver opening remarks. Dr. Polia, you have the floor.

Thank you, President of ECOSOC. Good afternoon, buenas tardes, and thank you to all the delegates in the room, to all young people in the room. It's really my pleasure to be with you to open this plenary session on youth leadership. Again, I think this is a space to recognize also the leadership of the President of ECOSOC for convening this whole 3 days and all the team working behind the scenes to make this forum happen. And specifically, today's session, this session we are starting at this point, it's about bringing together 2 critical dimensions. On one hand, youth leadership in challenging contexts, and on the second hand, the journey from civic into institutional influence. And that's where we want this conversation to be focused, on how we move from consultation to influence, how we move from activation to institutional transformation. But before getting into the discussion, I want to acknowledge something which is real and it's hard. Which is that this year, once again, too many young people are not in this room, are not with us. Some of them because of conflict, some of them because of displacement, others because of visa restrictions, or just because there are structural inequalities that don't allow them to have access to these rooms. I have to say, this is something even in first person for our office, because of some of these restrictions, some members of our own Youth Reference Group are not here in the room. And I have to say, this is a question of access, and it's a question of which voices are heard in global decision-making. So I know that every young person intervening today will bring this to our attention, and even some of you are not here, I'm sure that through your engagement, their voices, those realities will be considered. And allow me just to say a few words in Spanish because I think very often the language barrier is something that we encounter in these spaces. And the fact is that when we talk about participation, not all youth have the same opportunity to participate. And those who find themselves in conflict countries, conflict zones, are the ones who face the greatest barriers. And it is precisely These situations, these discussions that should draw our attention, because meaningful participation means inclusion and access. But if we are committed to leaving no one behind, so let's bring these situations to our discussion today. Dear youth in the room, dear decision-makers in the room, dear civil society actors, across the world young people are showing us that they are not waiting for permission to be invited. Young people are showing us that they are already leading on their way, and amid shrinking civic space, Young people are organizing, young people are advocating, young people are shaping change. And in this call is where the tension needs to be. While youth engagement is growing, at the same time, youth participation in formal structures is still very low. And far beyond where we should be. If we consider those young people in parliaments, the number is still marginal. If we consider those young people with an Assistant Secretary-General in the UN role, it's a marginal number still. And behind this number, what we have is structural barriers. Is limited access to resources, is restrictive legal frameworks and political systems that are not really designed to include youth. But we're also seeing, paradoxically, the power of youth. Youth-led movements transforming governments, youth-led movements redefining how participation happens. Young people shaping narratives, demanding accountability, demanding the end of corruption, demanding investments on those topics that are the topics needed by communities. So as we have this conversation, it's about also exposing the limits of our current institutions. And this is a tension to have, but it's positive we are having that tension. It's positive we are having that openness to discuss and recognize it. Because when institutions do not create meaningful pathways for participation, it's not that young people are not engaging. They're finding other alternatives to be heard. But it's institutions, the ones that are losing that capacity for creativeness, for innovation. So if we really want to have institutions that are trusted, we need to get into the decision of sharing power. It's more than creating space, it's sharing power. It's about investing in youth-led solutions. It's about ensuring that participation leads to real influence. And it's about recognizing also that in the current world, the digital space is a civic space. The digital space, it's a political space, and that we need to protect youth activists not only in the traditional spaces but also in the digital space. So, as the UN, We take this seriously. We are committed to drive what we can do. We are committed to create more convening spaces for this agenda to move forward, but also we are committed to implement this agenda through the implementation of the core principles of meaningful youth participation across intergovernmental meetings of the UN, but also in the day-to-day of our our UN country teams implement initiatives with and for youth through the UN Youth Strategy. So as we start this session, please, let's keep with us one concrete question: how do we ensure that the leadership we see in the communities, that the leadership we are seeing in the movements, that the leadership we are seeing in online spaces is transformed into leadership in our institutions. Because ultimately, the goal is not only to recognize youth leadership, it is to ensure that youth leadership shapes the decisions that define our collective future. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Sunita. The moderator asked whether participation today translates into real influence. My honest answer is not automatically, and I am proof of both sides of that. Too often, young people are invited into rooms to be heard but not trusted to shape outcomes. Real participation really happens when we see young people with resources, power, and follow-through. At Amnesty International, thanks to a global children and youth strategy which was co-led by young people, we're actively walking towards youth empowerment. Currently, at least one-third of our Global Assembly delegates have at least— are at least 25 years old, and that matters because participation is ultimately about giving the space for youth to influence the priorities that we have. So one of the things that becomes a problem is defining fragility or crisis or what's complex as if any of that existed in a neat category. It doesn't at countries, it doesn't in communities, it doesn't even for us as individuals, but But I think what we're seeing across the board is that the risks are escalating, they're connecting in different ways, they're making it more costly from a human toll first and foremost, but also from a financial toll. And no one knows this better than young people that are living in contexts that are defined as crisis or fragile affected. So in those contexts, 3 quarters of the population is under the age of 30. It is literally a youth movement from inside these countries. And armed conflicts are more frequent and more deadly than ever. I don't need to tell anybody in this room that, but some of the statistics that I still think are important for us to ground the conversation we're having today— armed conflicts have gone from somewhere over 6,000 armed conflicts in the early 2000s to 20,000 today, and that's defined as organized groups that are using armed force, whether within or across borders. But a statistic that's even more concerning, if you count the number of individual violent events, and you think about the way that might impact you, your communities, and the way that you can leverage change, that number is more than 230,000 individual violent incidents just over the 2024 to 2025 period. We know that most of these contexts are also impacted by climate change, and then the highest price is always paid, and, and my colleagues have mentioned the same thing, by those that aren't making the decision to fight in the first place. So countries, again, with that high-intensity conflict, their economies contract by 20 percentage points in 5 years. And I think that's what we need to do in our actions today. So, one of the things that I want to come back to is the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda. So, the core message, which has remained over the years, is still valid, and that's that we can't see young people through a lens of risk. We need to recognize young people for what they are, which is political actors, peacebuilders, drivers of change. And so on the point on elections, indeed, elections matter, but for many people today, and certainly those that we're working with, they're no longer the primary channel for political agency. The action is in digital activism, in social movements, and in community organizing. What I want to come back to just as we close, and I look forward to hearing from you in the session that's going to follow, is that we have a real challenge of linking participation to opportunity, to come back to the first question that we were asked. It requires taking the economy seriously. One of the major things that we're focusing on, and our administrator has come back to this over and over again, is jobs and decent work. It is impossible to build any kind of peace and any kind of stability on an empty future. And again, as much as I know that I'm telling that to people that would understand it very clearly, clearly, that's an area that we need to focus more fully in the way that we take our work forward at the UN and support you in your endeavors. And so, I want to close with 2 reflections, and it's for you in the room, and it's for those that was mentioned at the beginning that couldn't join us today. And the first is that I don't want to congratulate young people in conflicts, in crisis, in complex settings for their resilience, and I really think it's something collectively we have to stop. because surviving injustice is not an achievement to celebrate. We need, please, to put justice at the center of everything that we're doing. We certainly believe that at the UN, and I hope it's the same in the work that you're doing. And very much along those lines, I don't think we should be calling young people, all of you in the room, the solution. Your drive and commitment is not a substitute for institutions like the UN, like the room that you're in, and the member states that it represents, who need to do their jobs So, with the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda, we've long noted that this is not a warning about young people, this is a warning to institutions. And the alternative to meaningful engagement, as we've seen in our work with young people around the world, is not silence, it's disruption. And I think we're experiencing seeing that in many ways today. And this eroded legitimacy will be a challenge for the multilateral system, impacting all of us, all of our collective futures together. So I hope that we can name and hold account where it's required. I hope that we can be really clear and specific in what the challenges are and where you have an opportunity, where you have an opening, where you have a passion, where you have the skills, and then we work together to make meaningful change, change the outcomes, not just the process. Thank you.

Thank you very much for your wonderful insights. I would like to bring back Rodrigo once again. What are some of the less visible or personal costs that young people face when entering institutional spaces for the first time? And how are grassroots and informal movements reshaping participation?

I come from Buraco, which is a marginalized neighborhood in Portugal, and today I'm here speaking at the United Nations. That transition involved many costs, and it still does. I was raised by a single mother in a low-income migrant family, as I hope many of you here— I really hope so— and I'm a first-generation college student. So there was no roadmap for me to arrive in rooms like this one. For many of us, especially those coming from working-class migrant, racialized, queer, or otherwise excluded backgrounds, entering institutional spaces means constantly adjusting ourselves. You think about how you speak, you think about how you dress, you think about whether you sound polished enough, formal enough, institutional enough. You do not just enter a room, you are constantly translating yourself. And then there is also the material cost. Participation is often celebrated in principle, we know that, but rarely supported in practice. Time costs money, unpaid opportunities cost money, travel costs money, formal clothes— I see many people in suits here, and me myself, I'm wearing a suit now— but that also costs a lot of money, right? So when you have to think about all of this, you see that exclusion in fact is not always a closed door. Many times it is an open door that still costs too much to get to and then to walk through. That is why when we speak about youth participation we have to ask ourselves, participation for whom and at whose expense? Because if participation depends on exhaustion, on sacrifice, on unpaid resilience, then that is not truly participation. That is not what should be inclusive. That is also why grassroots and youth-led movements have been reshaping their action and why they matter so much. They remind us that legitimacy does not only exist within the walls of institutions such as this one. When formal spaces remain inaccessible or symbolic, young people will continue to organize elsewhere, to build power elsewhere, and rightly so. So to anyone here in the room who also feels like an outsider, like I do, I want to tell you this: do not shrink yourself to fit the room, and once you enter in it, you own it and you belong to it. So to the policymakers and ministers here in the room, if you truly believe in leaving no one behind, Then do not just invite young people in. Be intentional about who you invite. Be intentional about whose realities are represented and who is still missing. Trust us, resources, because the real measure of inclusion is not whether we have some few exceptional young people managing to make it and breaking through, but whether the next one arrives with a little less struggle and a little more certainty that they do belong. We're not asking to make it easier, we're just asking to make it fairer. So if there is one thing that I want to leave you with is that many of us arrive in these places alone, but we carry the sacrifices and the struggles of communities that raised us and the responsibility to make the path wider for the ones who are still getting in. As Sam Cooke once sang, It has been a very long time coming, but I know and I'm very sure that a change is going to come. Thank you.

my generation works in a context where realities move faster than the systems meant to respond to them. Youth leadership is not waiting to emerge.
